items.prompt: Which task is deep work in Sam's Saturday?
choices: Building the argument of the hard essay
Telling a housemate where the scissors are
Replying to a message about dinner time
items.explanation: Deep work is effortful, focused, and costly to interrupt. A quick answer is shallow.

items.prompt: Which task is shallow work in Sam's Saturday?
choices: Planning the structure of the whole essay
Rewriting the essay's hardest paragraph
Saying what time dinner will be ready
items.explanation: Shallow work is low-focus and logistical, and it survives being done in short bursts.

items.prompt: What defines deep work in this unit?
choices: Any task that takes longer than an hour on the calendar
Focused effort on a demanding task with no switching
Work done alone in a quiet room with the door shut
items.explanation: Depth comes from sustained focus on something demanding, not from length or location.

items.prompt: What defines shallow work in this unit?
choices: Easy tasks that are not worth doing for a serious person
Low-focus logistical tasks that need no sustained attention
Any task that takes under five minutes to finish fully
items.explanation: Shallow means low in focus demand, not low in value.

items.prompt: Does this unit say shallow work should be eliminated?
choices: No, it is necessary and only needs a better place
Yes, because every minute of it harms the deep work
Yes, but only on the days a hard task is due soon
items.explanation: Shallow work such as helping people still has to happen; the question is when.

items.prompt: Was helping a housemate a waste of Sam's time?
choices: Yes, any help given during a work day is a waste
Yes, because Sam should have refused all requests
No, helping was fine; its timing was the problem
items.explanation: The unit separates the value of the help from the cost of when it landed.

items.prompt: Why do deep and shallow work both feel like working?
choices: Both draw on exactly the same amount of attention
Both produce the same kind of finished result by evening
Both occupy the day and use effort, but differ in depth
items.explanation: Feeling busy says nothing about which kind of work filled the time.

items.prompt: Which pair is deep, then shallow?
choices: Answering a quick text, then scheduling a short call
Drafting a hard argument, then answering a quick text
Filing a receipt, then replying to a short reminder
items.explanation: Only the first pair has a demanding task followed by a low-focus one.

items.prompt: Sam spends an hour on each of: untangling the essay's central argument, replying to five short messages, and booking a dentist visit. Which classification is correct?
choices: Three hours of deep work, since all of it needed effort
Two hours of deep work and one hour of shallow work
One hour of deep work and two hours of shallow work
Three hours of shallow work, since none produced a finished essay
items.explanation: Only the argument demanded sustained focus and had context worth protecting. Messages and booking are logistical, so they are shallow however long they take.
items.reference:
Deep vs. shallow
🧠 deep: effortful, no switching (the hard essay)
💬 shallow: low-focus, logistical (a quick answer)
⏱️ the issue is where shallow work lands, not that it exists
Why: the two kinds feel the same while doing them but cost very different amounts when cut off partway.
items.learnMore:
Deep work and shallow work

Both kinds are real work. Deep work builds up context that is expensive to lose; shallow work can be done in short bursts with little loss. The skill is placing each kind where it costs least.

Common mistake

Treating shallow work as worthless, or treating every task as equally easy to pause.
items.reflection: Think of a recent day. Which task was your deep work, and what kind of shallow work usually landed on top of it?

items.prompt: A friend says 'shallow work is a waste, so I refuse every request while I write.' What does this unit say about that approach?
choices: It is right, because every shallow task weakens deep work
It overcorrects: shallow work is needed, only its timing hurts
It is right during deadlines but wrong on ordinary days
It is wrong, because shallow work is just as valuable to protect
items.explanation: The unit keeps shallow work and moves it. Refusing everything trades one problem for others, such as blocking a teammate.

items.prompt: What is attention residue?
choices: The tiredness left after a long day of focused work
Part of your attention stuck on the task you just left
The notes you keep after finishing a hard task
items.explanation: Residue is lingering attention, which is why a short break still costs more than its length.

choices: The time and effort to rebuild context after a switch
The price of buying a tool for a different task
The delay before a colleague replies to a message
items.explanation: It is the work of getting back to the earlier depth and speed.

choices: About fifteen minutes
About twenty minutes
Under a minute

240, roughly one every 2 minutes
24, roughly one every 20 minutes

Sam was always working, just mostly rebuilding focus
Sam was working far too slowly on every task

Yes, because Sam answered housemates too politely

items.explanation: Effort does not remove the rebuilding cost that each switch causes.

choices: Yes, they are exact averages across every person
Yes, they were measured in a famous lab study
No, they are stated assumptions to show the mechanism

It ignores the far longer rebuilding after each answer
The 12 minutes is fine, but housemates should ask fewer questions
The 12 minutes is correct, so the essay must be too hard
items.explanation: The count covers only direct handling. Rebuilding context after each answer is the larger, unrecorded cost.
items.reference:
Why a quick question costs more
🧠 deep work builds context
💬 interruption: under 1 min to answer
🔁 residue: ~15 min to rebuild (assumed)
📉 the rebuilding never shows up as a line item

items.reflection: When you were last pulled away from something hard, how long did it take before you felt fully back in?

The sender's time and the receiver's time together

The refocus time after the interruption

choices: The seconds spent reading and answering
The minutes spent rebuilding your context
The effort lost to residual attention
items.explanation: Handling is visible in messages; refocusing is not.

choices: Attention residue, then refocusing
A rest period and then the next task
An immediate return to full depth

About 3 hours
About 15 minutes

No, only machines can interrupt you
items.explanation: Self-interruption triggers the same residue as any other.

items.prompt: Why can a person honestly say 'I only spent 12 minutes' and still be wrong?
choices: They counted handling and left out refocusing
They measured the wrong day of the week
They counted minutes that were not real work
items.explanation: The honest count covers only the visible part of the cost.

items.prompt: A teammate answers 40 messages in a day, 20 seconds each, about 13 minutes. They say 'so interruptions cost me 13 minutes.' What is the best correction?
choices: That is handling only; the refocus after each is separate
That is too high, since the messages were all very short ones
That is correct, since the cost equals the time spent
That is too low only if the messages were all long
items.explanation: Total cost adds the refocus time after each message. The 13 minutes covers handling alone.
items.reference:
Two parts of one interruption
✋ direct handling: seconds, visible
🔁 refocus: minutes, invisible
➕ true cost = both parts added
📏 refocus is usually the larger part
Why: judging by handling time alone misses most of what an interruption costs.
items.learnMore:
The two-part cost

Cost of an interruption equals the time to handle it plus the time to get back to depth. Because the second part is not recorded anywhere, people consistently undercount.

Common mistake

Believing a short interruption must be a cheap one.
items.reflection: Where in your own routine do you only count the visible part of what something costs?

items.prompt: What happens when interruptions arrive more often than the refocus time?
choices: You never reach full depth on the task
You reach full depth faster after each one
You reach depth, but only on easy tasks
items.explanation: If the gap is shorter than the rebuild, you are always mid-rebuild.

items.prompt: With a 15-minute refocus and a 10-minute gap, how many deep minutes in the day?
items.explanation: The gap is below the refocus time, so no depth is ever reached.

items.prompt: With a 15-minute refocus and a 20-minute gap, how many deep minutes in a 480-minute day?
items.explanation: (20 minus 15) divided by 20 is a quarter of 480, which is 120.

items.prompt: With a 15-minute refocus and a 30-minute gap, how many deep minutes in a 480-minute day?
items.explanation: (30 minus 15) divided by 30 is a half of 480, which is 240.

items.prompt: With a 15-minute refocus and a 60-minute gap, how many deep minutes in a 480-minute day?
items.explanation: (60 minus 15) divided by 60 is three quarters of 480, which is 360.

items.prompt: In the demo, which two sliders does the model use?
choices: Number of tasks and number of coworkers
Length of the day and number of breaks
Minutes between interruptions and refocus minutes
items.explanation: The demo varies the gap between interruptions and the refocus time.

items.prompt: Which row of L2's table describes frequent interruptions?

Full depth reached quickly after each ping
Little or no time at full depth, always mid-refocus
items.explanation: Frequent pings keep the person in rebuild mode.

items.prompt: Does frequency matter more than the length of each interruption?
choices: No, only the length of each interruption matters
Yes, it decides how much depth ever happens
No, neither one affects the amount of depth
items.explanation: L2 says frequency, relative to refocus time, is what decides the day.

items.prompt: With a 15-minute refocus time, a team cuts interruptions from every 12 minutes to every 15 minutes. What do they gain in deep minutes?
choices: About 100 minutes, since the gap grew by 3 minutes
About 240 minutes, since the gap is now exactly refocus
About 360 minutes, since depth now appears in each gap
Nothing, since both gaps are within the refocus time
items.explanation: Both gaps are at or below 15 minutes, so the model gives 0 deep minutes in each case.
items.reference:
Gap vs. refocus time (15 min refocus, 480 min day)
🔁 gap 5, 10, 15 min: 0 deep minutes
📈 gap 20 min: 120 deep minutes
📈 gap 30 min: 240 deep minutes
📈 gap 60 min: 360 deep minutes
Why: depth only appears once the gap between interruptions exceeds the refocus time.
items.learnMore:
Frequency versus length

The formula is (gap minus refocus) divided by gap, times the day. When the gap is no longer than the refocus time, nothing survives. Beyond it, each extra minute of gap helps a lot at first.

Common mistake

Thinking that halving the interruptions halves the damage; near the threshold the effect is far larger.
items.reflection: Where in your week is the gap between interruptions close to the time you need to get back in?

items.prompt: Where should a protected block be placed?

items.prompt: What follows a protected block in L2's fix?

A second block with no gap between them
items.explanation: The batched window clears the waiting questions.

items.prompt: Who decides when shallow work happens in a protected day?

The loudest request of the day

items.explanation: In a reactive day, whatever arrives first decides; protection reverses that.

items.prompt: A manager says 'protecting deep-work blocks means we answer fewer messages.' What is the best response?

Yes, but only the unimportant messages are skipped

No, the blocks should be shorter than the catching-up windows
items.explanation: The fix reorders shallow work. The count answered stays the same; the interruptions inside blocks disappear.
items.reference:
Reactive day vs. protected day
🔀 reactive: shallow work lands all day
🛡️ protected: blocks on the calendar, set windows for catching up
📦 the total shallow work stays the same
✂️ only the number of broken-depth moments shrinks
Why: the fix changes when shallow work happens, not how much of it there is.
items.learnMore:
Protecting blocks

A protected block is planned ahead, with notifications off and a note to the people likely to interrupt. Shallow work moves to a window right after. Planning matters because 'when it is quiet' fails the first time something comes up.

Common mistake

Believing protection means doing less shallow work, or protecting time only when it happens to be quiet.
items.reflection: What is one stretch of your week you could protect, and what would you put in the catching-up window after it?
